p.title: D-NOMINATE After 10 Years: A Comparative Update to Congress: A Political Economic History of Roll Call Voting

ext.title: D-NOMINATE After 10 Years: A Comparative Update to Congress
ext.venue: SSRN working paper, 27 September 1999 (SSRN abstract 1154162). Metadata hint verified: title, authors, year and SSRN id match the PDF. No journal version is stated in the text.
ext.document_type: Working paper (SSRN), update to the book Congress: A Political-Economic History of Roll Call Voting (Poole and Rosenthal, 1997)
ext.coverage: Whole text read: all 1,743 lines of the extracted text (46,871 chars), in one pass. Annotation JSON read in full: 57 Paul Goff markup items (56 highlights and 1 FreeText). Colors: 48 yellow, 7 green (p.2, p.17, p.19, p.20 x4), 1 pink (p.17). Figures 1-10 are not present in the extracted text (only "about here" placeholders), so claims resting on those figures cannot be checked from this text. Topic check against the brief: legislators (ideal points, chamber-level polarization) and elections/realignment (1994 shift, Civil Rights realignment of the South) are covered; donors and primary races appear only in one passage (p.17). Lobbying, networks, path-finding, allocation, persuasion/turnout and text measurement are not addressed. Covered text in paul_markup is paraphrased, not quoted (copyright rule). Only one short quote is given (copyright rule).
ext.research_question: Have the trends identified in Congress (1997) toward polarization and one-dimensionality in roll call voting continued through the 105th Congress, and does the 1994 Republican takeover represent a sharp break? Secondary: do DW-NOMINATE and alternative scaling methods recover essentially the same legislator positions, and how does the U.S. Congress fit the spatial model compared with other legislatures? (Abstract p.2; Sec. 1 p.3.)
ext.theory: Basic spatial theory of ideology (Ordeshook 1976; Hinich and Pollard 1981; Enelow and Hinich 1984; Hinich and Munger 1994): legislators have ideal points in a low-dimensional policy space and choose the outcome closer to them. Dynamic extension: legislator coordinates are polynomial functions of time (Appendix eq. A1, p.19). Roll call utility is a normal-error probit over a Gaussian-type distance with dimension salience weights (eqs. A2-A4, p.20).
ext.data: U.S. House and Senate roll calls, Congresses 1-105 (1789-1998). Unit: legislator-roll call choice (Yea or Nay; abstentions discarded, endnote 9, p.30). Legislators included if they cast at least 25 votes in at least one Congress (endnote 1, p.30). House: 38,740 scalable roll calls, 10,208 scalable representatives, 10,495,639 choices (Table 1, p.23). Senate: 41,165 roll calls, 1,794 senators, 2,697,691 choices (Table 1, p.24). Joint House-Senate scaling: 79,905 roll calls, 11,389 unique legislators, 13,193,330 choices, with 613 members serving in both chambers as "glue" (Table 3, p.27; p.10). Presidents Eisenhower through Clinton included as members of both chambers using CQ presidential support roll calls (p.10). Comparison sets (Table 4, p.28-29): 105th House (946 roll calls, 443 legislators), 105th Senate (486, 101), Third and Fourth European Parliament, 1841 British Parliament, French National Assembly 1951-56, Czech Parliament 1993-97, 1995 Polish Parliament, UN General Assembly sets.
ext.method: DW-NOMINATE (dynamic, weighted, nominal three-step estimation): normal (probit) errors replacing D-NOMINATE's logit errors; per-dimension salience weights w_k; legislator coordinates polynomial in time, estimated as constant (v=0) and linear (v=1) only (p.5-6, Appendix p.19-20). Estimated by maximum likelihood over the joint choice likelihood (eq. A4, p.20). Comparators: Poole's non-parametric optimal classification (rank ordering that maximizes correct classification; one dimension only; Poole 1997, 2000), Heckman-Snyder factor analysis (p.9). Fit measured by percent correctly classified, APRE, and geometric mean probability (Table 1 notes, p.24-25). Party polarization measured by mean within- and between-party pairwise distances (Figs 7-8, p.14) and percent party overlap (Fig 9, p.15). Joint scaling of both chambers estimated with optimal classification (Table 3, p.27).
ext.identification: Not a causal design; this is measurement of ideal points. Ideal points are identified by maximum likelihood across roll calls with the salience weight for dimension 1 set to one and the probit error variance normalized to 1 (p.8). Linear trends are estimated for legislators serving at least 3 (or 5) Congresses; the authors concede the 3-Congress threshold lets random walkers appear linear, which biases toward the polynomial models (p.6). Joint House-Senate scaling assumes the 613 glue members hold fixed positions across chambers (p.10); the authors call this "reasonably supported" from the classification drop of about 1 point (p.11-12).
ext.scope: Population: all roll call votes and members of the U.S. House and Senate, 1789-1998 (Congresses 1-105). Substantive focus: Post-Reconstruction Democrat/Republican party system, 1879-1998, with extra attention to recent Congresses (p.12). Cross-national comparison (Sec. 6, p.16-17): a few legislatures at single time spans. Institution: the U.S. Congress plus selected parliaments. Era: Post-Reconstruction and modern polarization (1879-1998).

key_findings.finding: On Congresses 1-99, 2D linear DW-NOMINATE nearly reproduces D-NOMINATE: correct classification 85.4 (House) and 84.6 (Senate) vs 85.2 and 84.5; dimension-1 coordinate correlations .977 House and .974 Senate; dimension-2 .923 House and .901 Senate.
Adding Congresses 100-105 raises correct classification by about 0.6 points in the House and 0.3 in the Senate; recent Congresses fit the model better than earlier ones.
The second dimension adds under 2 points of classification in the House and about 2.5 in the Senate over one dimension.
key_findings.numbers: House 1D constant 83.82 vs 2D constant 85.65; Senate 81.46 vs 84.04

key_findings.finding: The linear (time-varying) model is not a striking improvement over the constant model; lowering the linear threshold from 5 to 3 Congresses adds about 0.1 (House) and 0.3 (Senate) points.
key_findings.numbers: House 2D constant 85.65 vs linear 85.96 (5-Cong threshold) and 86.08 (3-Cong); Senate 84.04 vs 84.40 and 84.70; about 0.3 points for linear over constant

key_findings.finding: Unidimensionality trend: the second dimension now adds under 1 percent of improvement over the first in both chambers; the authors call the post-early-1970s trend dramatic.
key_findings.location: Sec. 3, p.7-8 (Figs 1B, 2B are not in the text)

key_findings.finding: Utility-function estimates for DW-NOMINATE: second-dimension salience weight w-squared is .3160 (House, linear) and .3087 (Senate, linear); beta is 4.125 (House, 2D linear) and 4.078 (Senate, 2D linear). Standard errors are acknowledged as not econometrically correct.
key_findings.numbers: w^2 .3160 House, .3087 Senate; beta 4.125 House, 4.078 Senate (2D linear)

key_findings.finding: Optimal classification (1D, rank order maximizing correct votes) beats 1D DW-NOMINATE constant by about 2 points in the House and about 3 in the Senate, yet the two produce similar rank orders.
key_findings.numbers: Spearman .960 (n=10,208) House and .981 (n=1,794) Senate; .972 (n=5,018) and .985 (n=1,183) for members with 500+ votes; joint OC 85.60% correct, APRE .567; House 85.98, Senate 84.51

key_findings.finding: Joint House-Senate rank order (613 glue members, presidents included as members of both chambers) reproduces the chamber-separate DW-NOMINATE orders closely; the common members are classified about 1 point worse under joint scaling.
key_findings.numbers: Spearman .952 (House, n=10,208), .965 (Senate, n=1,794); .960 and .969 for 500+ votes; 85.46% (separate House), 85.10% (separate Senate), 84.54% (joint) for the 613; cross-chamber rank correlation .790 (270 with 500+ votes: .846)

key_findings.finding: Party means: cross-time correlation of Republican dimension-1 means is .911 and Democratic .837; cross-chamber correlation of party means .722. Median-rank correlations across chambers: Republicans .888, Democrats .850.

Polarization (between minus within party distances) fell from the early 20th century to WWII, was stable until the late 1970s, and has risen steadily since; Congresses 100-105 accelerate the trend smoothly, with no jump after the 1994 freshman class.
key_findings.numbers: qualitative; no numbers in the text

key_findings.finding: Party overlap has fallen to near zero: no overlap in the past 3 Senates and under 1.5 percent in both chambers for the past 5 Congresses. The 1940s-late-1970s hump is attributed to the Civil Rights split in the Democratic Party.

The current polarization of parties is comparable to the Federalist/Jeffersonian system of 1800 but well below late-19th/early-20th-century levels; Fig 10 covers normal two-party periods only and excludes the pre-Civil War and Civil War decade.

Cross-national fit: the 105th House (one-dimensional 88.2% correct, APRE .644; two-dimensional 89.2%, .674) and Senate (88.0%, .642; 88.5%, .660) fit the spatial model about as well as most legislatures. On APRE only the Czech Parliament (.770), the 1841 British Parliament (.651) and the French National Assembly 1951-56 (.818) fit better.

Party per se is said to explain little roll call voting beyond the spatial model; parties are spatially adjacent ideological coalitions; members may respond to donors and primaries as well as party pressure. These claims rest on a cited 1999 working paper not presented here.
key_findings.location: Sec. 6, p.17 (cites McCarty, Poole and Rosenthal 1999)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: the trends in Congress (1997) have continued unabated; polarization is far from over, but is not as severe as in earlier eras, and no current issue appears capable of destabilizing the system as slavery did.

limitations: Abstentions are forced into Yea or Nay and discarded as missing (endnote 9, p.30); abstention modeling is left to future work.

Standard errors for DW-NOMINATE utility parameters are not econometrically correct because the full outer-product matrix (about 180,000 by 180,000 for the House) was not inverted; the authors expect the values to change little (p.8).
The 3-Congress linear-trend threshold lets random walkers appear linear, biasing toward the polynomial models (p.6).
Optimal classification was done only in one dimension; the two-dimensional version was deferred (p.9).

Joint House-Senate scaling assumes that members keep fixed positions across chambers; the authors call this reasonably supported, but the 613 glue members lose about 1 point of classification under joint scaling (p.10-11).

The 100th Congress was scaled separately and transformed to fit earlier Congresses (endnote 7, p.30). The text reports the 1-99 Senate classification as 84.6 while Table 1 (linear, 3-Cong, 1-99) reports 84.42; minor discrepancy.

The cross-national claim that only the Czech, 1841 British and French National Assembly fit better than the 105th Congress holds on APRE and classification jointly. On classification alone, the Third and Fourth European Parliaments (89.8, 89.4) and the 1995 Polish Parliament (88.9) exceed the 105th House's 88.2 in one dimension (Table 4, p.28-29; text p.17).
Figures 1-10 are not in the extracted text, so the trend claims resting on them (Figs 1B, 2B, 7-10) cannot be verified here.

The party-discipline argument depends on a 1999 working paper (McCarty, Poole and Rosenthal) that is cited but not presented (p.17). The paper contains no causal analysis, so the 1994 break is assessed only descriptively (p.14-15).
references_of_note: Poole and Rosenthal (1997) Congress: A Political-Economic History of Roll Call Voting, OUP. The book this paper updates; DW-NOMINATE and the spatial reinterpretation of Congress.
McCarty, Poole and Rosenthal (1997) Income Redistribution and the Realignment of American Politics, AEI. Source of DW-NOMINATE and the redistribution/race dimension story.

McCarty, Poole and Rosenthal (1999) The Hunt for Party Discipline in Congress, working paper. Cited for the claim that donors and primaries shape ideal points beyond party (p.17). Relevant to elections and lobbying-adjacent pressure.
Krehbiel (1993) Where's the Party? British Journal of Political Science 23:235-66. Parties as spatially adjacent ideological coalitions (p.17).
Carmines and Stimson (1989) Issue Evolution: Race and the Transformation of American Politics, Princeton. Realignment of the South toward the Republicans (p.12-13). Relevant to elections.
McCarty and Poole (1995) Veto power and legislation, Journal of Law, Economics and Organization 11:282-312. Source of the CQ presidential support roll calls used to score presidents (p.10).
Hinich and Munger (1994) Ideology and the Theory of Political Choice, Michigan. Basic spatial theory of ideology (p.2, endnote 2).
Heckman and Snyder (1997) Rand Journal of Economics 28:142-189. Factor-analytic alternative to NOMINATE (p.9).
Poole (1997, 2000) optimal classification / non-parametric unfolding, Political Analysis (forthcoming). Benchmark used in Sec. 4 (p.9-11).
Londregan (2000) Political Analysis 8(1). One-dimensional preferred-point estimator for small legislatures (p.9).
Poole and Rosenthal (1984) The Polarization of American Politics, Journal of Politics 46:1061-79. Earlier polarization measure (p.14).
measures: Percent correctly classified (House, Senate, joint; per Congress and per model; Tables 1, 3, 4)
APRE (aggregate proportional reduction in error; Table 1 notes, p.24)
Geometric mean probability GMP = exp(log-likelihood / N) (Table 1 note d, p.25)
Salience weight w-squared and utility scale beta (Table 2, p.26)
Spearman rank correlations of legislator orders, with and without members with 500+ votes (p.10-11)
Pearson correlations of dimension coordinates (p.7) and of party means / median ranks (p.13-14)
Within- and between-party mean pairwise distances (p.14, Figs 7-8)
Percent party overlap: share of a party's members closer to the opposing mean (p.15, Fig 9)
Normalized joint rank (rank divided by 11,389) for median ranks (p.13)

short_quotes.quote: We have a polarized, unidimensional Congress.

rel.summary_md:
Poole and Rosenthal update their 1997 roll-call study through the 105th Congress (1789-1998) using DW-NOMINATE, a dynamic probit spatial model of legislator ideal points. Four results matter here. First, legislator positions are close to fixed over a career: the linear time-trend model adds only about 0.3 points of classification over the constant model (House 85.65 to 85.96; Senate 84.04 to 84.40). Second, Congress has become one-dimensional: the second dimension now adds under 1 percent. Third, party overlap on dimension 1 is near zero: under 1.5% in both chambers over the last five Congresses, and none in the last three Senates. Fourth, polarization rose smoothly, with no break at 1994. A non-parametric rank method produces nearly the same orders (Spearman .960 House, .981 Senate). The donor and primary claim that Paul highlighted in pink rests on a cited working paper that this text does not present.

For the system as built, the paper is a measurement baseline. It is not an engine input. DW-NOMINATE appears only as a control (fec/members/dw_control.py) and through per-Congress Nokken-Poole scores used as a criterion. The sharpest consequence is for the say-do gate's Path V. One CU-aligned final-passage vote counts as corroboration, and in a polarized, one-dimensional chamber that vote mostly records the member's party. A read-only check confirms strong party sorting in several categories (details in bearings). That check is UNVERIFIED. The paper also explains why drift-based susceptibility criteria have little true variance to detect. It argues for using an ideal-point control rather than a bare party dummy wherever party-confounded tiers are interpreted, as in the CFPB isolation. The paper does nothing for lobbying, money effects, pathfinding or allocation.

bearings.paper_claim: Roll-call voting is now essentially one-dimensional (dimension 2 adds under 1% classification), and party overlap on dimension 1 is under 1.5% in both chambers over the past 5 Congresses (none in the past 3 Senates). Final-passage votes therefore largely reveal a member's position on the party/ideology dimension.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3 p.7-8; Sec. 5 p.15 (Fig 9 not in extracted text)
bearings.system_side: Path V corroborates a Champion/Defender cell if the member cast a net-CU-aligned final-passage vote in that category, at lean >= 0.5 with n >= 1. One floor vote is treated as costly, issue-specific evidence. Read-only check on 2026-10-09 (UNVERIFIED, single path; window = current vote_category_lean.json; denominators = roster party counts from moneyball_core.party(), D 259 and R 271). Share of each party with Path V corroboration in a category: CFPB D 2% vs R 66%; Technology & Emerging D 7% vs R 97%; Examination & Supervision D 41% vs R 96%; CU Capital D 3% vs R 55%; Charter Modernization D 83% vs R 26%; NCUA Budget D 56% vs R 19%. Path V sorts strongly by party, so in these categories it may corroborate party-line voting rather than CU commitment.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's evidence ends at the 105th Congress (1998), and it says the trend continued unabated. Modern Voteview data (119th Congress) show even less overlap, so the qualification carries over more strongly today. It applies to final-passage votes, which are the most party-structured. Procedural or amendment votes on CU-specific provisions could still carry issue-specific signal. The party split above is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062) and is quoted stratified by party only.

bearings.paper_claim: Legislator positions are nearly static: the linear-trend model is not a striking improvement over the constant model (about 0.3 points of classification, House 85.65 to 85.96, Senate 84.04 to 84.40). The authors also say the 3-Congress threshold lets random walkers look linear, so even this small gain overstates real movement.
bearings.system_side: The binding unblock for the N susceptibility slot used per-Congress Nokken-Poole drift as the movement criterion (DW-NOMINATE dim 1 is frozen). The gate MISSed every candidate at n=441 and was recorded as a real verdict: no N signal on any observed criterion. The receptivity layer keeps N in the susc blend without demonstrated signal.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This bears on interpretation only. A well-powered n does not ensure true-score variance: if most drift is estimation noise around fixed ideal points, the criterion's reliability caps any correlation. That is consistent with the MISS but does not overturn it. The brain rule 'NOT more looks on drift' stands. The paper does not license a re-look; it supports the brain's listed alternative, a CU-specific vote-switch criterion.

bearings.paper_claim: Across 1789-1998, a constant ideal point per legislator classifies almost as well as a time-varying one (about 0.3 points of difference). Members rarely move on the main dimension during their careers.
bearings.system_side: MAXSHIFT was cut from 40 to 18 because money moves positions little. Defections are rare, and the terminal rungs (Champion, Opponent) are immune to money defection.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is indirect. The paper measures stability of general ideology, not CU-category stance, and has no money treatment, so it supports a low prior on position change rather than any particular MAXSHIFT or DTHRESH value. CU-specific stances off dimension 1 could move more than general ideology does.

bearings.paper_claim: Party is a near-perfect separator on dimension 1 (overlap under 1.5%), and party per se explains little beyond spatial position (p.17). The relevant control is the ideal point, not only the party label.
bearings.system_side: The CFPB-negative tiers were recorded as party-confounded (D 123 vs R 7 before isolation; D 98 vs R 0 after). The open question is whether party still predicts the tier once votes are controlled. A DW-NOMINATE dim1 and extremity loader already exists and is used for psychometric residualization, but not here.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies if roll-call ideology is the confound of interest. With near-zero party overlap, dim1 and party are almost collinear in the current Congress. The informative test is within-party (dim1 inside D), not a pooled model. A pooled coefficient would carry the UNSTRATIFIED label.

bearings.paper_claim: Within-party and between-party distances diverge after the late 1970s, so the most extreme members sit farthest from the opposing party's mean.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 5 p.14-15 (Figs 7-8 not in extracted text)
bearings.system_side: Cooperation v2 (cross-party tie share) is known to be extremity-confounded. dw_control.py records cooperation_v2_z vs |dim1| = -0.250 (n=532/533, 2026-07-10) and requires |dim1| as an explicit control for A.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This holds for the polarized modern Congress. The paper supplies the structural reason that the extremity control is needed; it does not test the cooperation measure itself.

bearings.paper_claim: Parties are spatially adjacent ideological coalitions, with near-zero overlap on dimension 1, so a two-group partition of roll-call behaviour should recover party almost exactly. Cross-party members are the few near the cutting line.
bearings.system_side: Diagnostic Aref-Neal frustration partition on the signed mention layer (member_references.json). It runs a party-recovery check at k=2 and treats cross-party assignments as hidden-coalition candidates. It is not consumed by the chain. The component description in the brief (R sdsm vote backbone) does not match the live code, which partitions the mention layer.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A benchmark, not a replacement. If the cross-party 'hidden coalition' candidates are simply the members with the most moderate DW-NOMINATE dim1 scores, the mention layer adds nothing beyond roll-call ideology. Checking candidates against |dim1| would show whether the mention layer carries new information. This would not reintroduce the DW-NOMINATE vote edges Paul rejected; it is a diagnostic comparison only.

bearings.paper_claim: The probit spatial choice model (eqs. A2-A3): P(Yea) = Phi(beta x [difference of Gaussian distances to the Yea and Nay outcomes]), with salience weights w_k. This maps a latent position to a vote probability (beta 4.125 House, 2D linear).
bearings.system_side: Fixed ten-band ladder (0.70/0.35/0.25/0.15/0.05/-0.05/-0.15/-0.35/-0.70) on signed raw scores. The open question is whether the band edges correspond to observable vote-probability thresholds on CU roll calls.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The probit link is the standard way to test whether band edges map to monotone vote probabilities. It needs a member x CU roll-call matrix with dates, which the brain records as not in the repo; vote_category_lean.json is aggregated. Paul marked this appendix 'Most important part'.

bearings.paper_claim: General roll-call behaviour collapses onto one dimension (dimension 2 adds under 1%).
bearings.system_side: Topic priority adds alpha (0.15 flip / 0.25 coalition) x the IMP-weighted stance on other topics (leave-one-topic-out). This assumes a member's CU orientation is shared across topics.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Unidimensionality would justify cross-topic borrowing only if CU categories load in the same direction on dimension 1. The Path V shares above (UNVERIFIED) show opposite party loadings: CFPB, Technology and Exam lean R, while Charter and NCUA Budget lean D. So CU 'orientation' is not the NOMINATE dimension, and leave-one-out borrowing across those categories could import party sign. Alpha is small, which limits the damage.

gaps_exposed: No CU-specific roll-call scaling. The system has no member x CU roll-call matrix with dates (the brain says it is not in the repo), so it cannot test whether CU stances sit on dimension 1 or on a separate CU dimension. The paper shows this is the decisive measurement question.

Say-do Path V counts a single final-passage vote (n >= 1) as costly-signal corroboration and does not condition on party or ideal point. In a polarized, one-dimensional chamber that largely corroborates party-line voting. A within-party or dim1-residualized vote criterion is missing.

The engine uses a binary party dummy for partisan physics (cpf_diffusion / cpf_pressure at moneyball_core.py:543-548). It never uses ideological distance, although DW-NOMINATE is already loaded for psychometric controls (dw_control.py). Ideological distance is the paper's preferred variable.
Party-confounded stance tiers (the CFPB axis) are not residualized on dim1 and extremity, although a loader exists.
Abstention is ignored both in the paper (endnote 9) and in Path V. Strategic abstention on CU votes is unmeasured.
flags: The Path V party split (CFPB D 2% vs R 66%, Technology D 7% vs R 97%, Exam D 41% vs R 96%, Charter D 83% vs R 26%) is new agent analysis from one read-only path on 2026-10-09 (window: current vote_category_lean.json; denominators D 259 and R 271 from moneyball_core.party()). It is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062) and is quoted only stratified by party.

The component description for melange-sna.signed-coalitions (R sdsm vote backbone) is stale. The live fec/network/signed_coalitions.py:8 partitions the signed mention layer (member_references.json). The brain records Paul's rejection of DW-NOMINATE vote edges (topics/2026-06-feature-cosponsor-and-sector-networks.md:93). Nothing here recommends reinstating them.

The paper's claim that members respond to donors and primaries (p.17, Paul's pink highlight) rests on an uncited-in-text 1999 working paper with no evidence presented. It must not be read as support for the competitiveness multiplier or for reciprocity, which is NOT validated (D-104..D-108).
Nokken-Poole drift: the paper's stability result is a reason to doubt the criterion's reliability, not a licence for another look. The brain rule 'NOT more looks on drift' stands.

The paper's rank correlations (.960/.981, .952/.965) are pooled across 1789-1998, spanning party systems and the Civil Rights realignment fault line. They are UNSTRATIFIED and should not be quoted as modern-era agreement.
The paper proposes no SNA edge rule. It does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, so neither rejected proposal is in play.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's two annotation records for this paper are bare citations with no takeaways. His PDF markup puts a FreeText note, 'Most important part', on the appendix, and green highlights on the polynomial time path (A1), the deterministic and stochastic utility terms, the salience weights, and the probit choice probability (A3). His interest is in the spatial choice model itself. The built system does not use that machinery in any engine component. DW-NOMINATE enters only as a residualization control (dw_control.py, behavior_panel.py, work_baseline.py) and through Nokken-Poole scores as a one-look criterion. The brain records that Paul rejected DW-NOMINATE vote edges for the network. His highlights on the 'no 1994 break' and polarization findings agree with how the system treats party: hard partisan physics, and party confounds flagged in the CFPB and cooperation measures. His pink highlight on donors and primaries is the weakest-evidenced claim in the paper. It should not be taken as support for money-responsiveness components. His notes are not stale so much as unconnected: the probit choice model he marked has never been tried as the mapping from stance bands to CU vote probabilities. That is the clearest use this paper offers.

related.why: Aref and Neal partition signed House networks and find the two-way split recovers party, with a hidden third coalition. That is consistent with this paper's near-zero party overlap. NOMINATE dim1 is the natural benchmark for whether their cross-party members are anything more than cutting-line moderates.
Earlier signed-partition study of congressional collaboration. Its partitions can be checked against DW-NOMINATE ideal points as a spatial baseline.

Bonica applies spatial scaling to donors and recipients (CFscores) and puts candidates on the same ideological dimension that DW-NOMINATE estimates from roll calls. This bears directly on the donors-and-primaries claim this paper leaves unevidenced.
Co-voting network centrality is built from the same House roll-call data. It is a network alternative to spatial ideal points for summarizing roll-call structure.
Studies legislative polarization, which this paper documents as a smooth trend in roll-call space. Noble and Turner add a presidential-leadership mechanism for how positions polarize.
